name: Tianwen-2
significance: Tianwen-2 was launched to resolve the disputed origin of Kamo'oalewa, a small, fast-rotating quasi-satellite of Earth whose orbital and spectral properties leave it unclear whether it is a fragment blasted off the Moon or an ordinary main-belt asteroid captured into Earth's vicinity. It is the first mission to attempt a sample return from a quasi-satellite, and it carries three distinct, untested-in-combination sampling systems -- hovering collection, touch-and-go, and a robotic anchor-and-attach method using drill-tipped arms -- so it can adapt to whatever surface cohesion its approach survey reveals. After a roughly 400-day cruise, the spacecraft rendezvoused with the roughly 20-meter, school-bus-sized Kamo'oalewa in mid-2026 and returned the first close-up images of the object, refining its shape and spin state. Sample collection is planned by 2027, with return to Earth expected in late 2027; analysis of the returned material is intended to settle the lunar-versus-asteroid-belt origin question, while an extended mission will go on to visit the main-belt comet 311P/PANSTARRS.
statusNote: Near-Earth asteroid sample return, then onward to a main-belt comet. This entry models only the confirmed primary target -- rendezvous with 469219 Kamo'oalewa, achieved 2026-06-07 after station-keeping first at 30,000 km then 2,000 km, with sample collection (touch-and-go plus anchor-and-attach, targeting 200-1,000g) underway through April 2027 and Earth return expected late November 2027. The comet extension -- an Earth gravity-assist flyby after sample drop-off, then on to comet 311P/PanSTARRS, arrival not expected until 2035-01 -- is not modeled here: those dates are still provisional this far out (the same reason Tianwen-4, MMX, and other not-yet-executed mission phases aren't modeled), matching how OSIRIS-REx's Apophis extension and Hayabusa2's Torifune extension are also left off past their primary target. Path calculated, not measured (drawn dashed): JPL Horizons has no ephemeris for Tianwen-2, so the path is built from published dates.

legs._comment: APPROXIMATION, not ephemeris: CNSA publishes no trajectory for Tianwen-2 and JPL Horizons has no target for it, so this cruise can't be anchored to real waypoints the way other split legs are. A single 2025-05-28 -> 2026-06-07 Lambert arc was clearly wrong -- the zero-revolution solver forced a ~1-year, ~1-lap transfer into an a=1.03/e=0.45 orbit dipping to 0.57 AU (inside Venus's orbit), while the target, quasi-satellite 469219 Kamo'oalewa, never leaves ~0.90-1.10 AU and stays near Earth. These 7 waypoints are synthetic: a smoothstep blend from Earth's position to Kamo'oalewa's at each date (generated 2026-11-17 from the app's own ephemerides), which is the neighborhood a low-thrust rendezvous with an Earth quasi-satellite actually stays in. Replace with real waypoints if a trajectory is ever published.
